concepts.title: Nature of Learning: Change Brought by Experience
concepts.definition: Learning is any relatively permanent change in behaviour or behaviour potential that results from experience or practice -- not from maturation, fatigue or drugs. It shows in doing, but also in knowing: changed capacity counts as learning even before it is performed.
concepts.key_idea: Learning is experience-written change -- relatively permanent, practice-made, and more than performance.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy105.txt nature sections (describe the nature of learning, change in behaviour through experience and practice, learning versus maturation)
question_patterns: define learning and state its essential features
in class 11 learning chapter: why is change from maturation not called learning
distinguish learning from performance with an example
what does relatively permanent mean in the definition of learning
give examples of learning beyond the classroom
is a change caused by drugs an instance of learning discuss

solution_steps.explain: Ask whether practice or experience produced the change; maturation and temporary states do not count.
The change must be relatively permanent, not a passing shift in energy or mood.
Learning may stay unperformed -- knowledge gained is learning even if behaviour has not yet shown it.

concepts.title: Classical and Operant Conditioning
concepts.definition: Conditioning explains learning by association and consequence. In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus paired repeatedly with a significant one comes to evoke its response -- Pavlov's dogs salivating to a bell. In operant conditioning behaviour is strengthened by reinforcement and weakened by punishment -- consequences shape future action.
concepts.key_idea: Learn by pairing, learn by payoff -- associations teach anticipation, consequences teach repetition.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy105.txt conditioning sections (classical conditioning pavlov, operant conditioning skinner, reinforcement punishment, shaping)
question_patterns: explain classical conditioning with pavlov's experiment
in class 11 learning chapter: how does operant conditioning differ from classical conditioning
define reinforcement and punishment with classroom examples
what is shaping of behaviour through successive approximations
identify stimulus and response in a given conditioning example
why does reinforcement work better than punishment in shaping behaviour

solution_steps.explain: Classical conditioning links a neutral stimulus to a meaningful one until the neutral alone triggers the response.
Operant conditioning follows behaviour with reinforcement or punishment, changing the odds of its repetition.
Reinforcing closer and closer approximations -- shaping -- can train skills no single trial could produce.

concepts.title: Observational Learning and Cognitive Forms of Learning
concepts.definition: Not all learning needs direct reinforcement. Observational learning copies models -- children imitate what they watch, for better or worse; insight learning solves problems by sudden reorganisation of the field; and verbal learning shows how words and associations are memorised. Cognition thus joins conditioning in the full picture.
concepts.key_idea: Watch, understand, reorganise -- learning also happens without reward, by example and by insight.
concepts.textbook_ref: kepy105.txt cognitive sections (observational learning modelling, insight learning, verbal learning, forms or types of learning)
question_patterns: explain observational learning with an example
in class 11 learning chapter: what is insight learning describe an experiment
how does modelling influence children's behaviour
distinguish trial and error learning from insight learning
what is verbal learning and how is it studied
compare the different forms of learning discussed in the chapter

solution_steps.explain: Observational learning acquires behaviour by attending to a model, retaining it and reproducing it when motivated.
Insight learning reorganises the problem suddenly -- the solution appears as a whole, as in Kohler's chimpanzee studies.
Verbal learning studies serial lists, paired associates and free recall -- the cognitive layer of human learning.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A child fears the dentist after one painful visit and now cries at the clinic's smell. Analyse the fear using classical conditioning.

solution_template.explain: Pain (unconditioned stimulus) produced fear (unconditioned response); the clinic smell was merely present.
Paired with pain, the smell became a conditioned stimulus now triggering fear by itself.
New, pain-free pairings with the same smell can gradually extinguish the conditioned fear.

worked_examples.question_pattern: After watching elders rudely interrupt, a child starts interrupting guests despite no reward. Explain this learning.

solution_template.explain: This is observational learning -- the child attended to models, retained their behaviour and reproduced it.

solution_template.action: note the absence of direct reward
solution_template.explain: No reinforcement was given to the child; the model's perceived status sufficed.
Models teach without teaching -- which is why adults' example is a permanent lesson.
